\section*{Question 6}

Let \(f\) be the function given by \(f(x)=e^{-x^{2}}\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Write the first four nonzero terms and the general term of the Taylor series for \(f\) about \(x=0\).
\item[(b)] Use your answer to part (a) to find \(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0} \frac{1-x^{2}-f(x)}{x^{4}}\).
\item[(c)] Write the first four nonzero terms of the Taylor series for \(\int_{0}^{x} e^{-t^{2}} d t\) about \(x=0\). Use the first two terms of your answer to estimate \(\int_{0}^{1 / 2} e^{-t^{2}} d t\).
\item[(d)] Explain why the estimate found in part (c) differs from the actual value of \(\int_{0}^{1 / 2} e^{-t^{2}} d t\) by less than \(\frac{1}{200}\).
\item[(a)]
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{-x^{2}} & =1+\frac{\left(-x^{2}\right)}{1!}+\frac{\left(-x^{2}\right)^{2}}{2!}+\frac{\left(-x^{2}\right)^{3}}{3!}+\cdots+\frac{\left(-x^{2}\right)^{n}}{n!}+\cdots \\
& =1-x^{2}+\frac{x^{4}}{2}-\frac{x^{6}}{6}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n} x^{2 n}}{n!}+\cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[(b)] \(\frac{1-x^{2}-f(x)}{x^{4}}=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{6}+\sum_{n=4}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1} x^{2 n-4}}{n!}\)
Thus, \(\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{1-x^{2}-f(x)}{x^{4}}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}\).
\item[(c)]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{x} e^{-t^{2}} d t & =\int_{0}^{x}\left(1-t^{2}+\frac{t^{4}}{2}-\frac{t^{6}}{6}+\cdots+\frac{(-1)^{n} t^{2 n}}{n!}+\cdots\right) d t \\
& =x-\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{5}}{10}-\frac{x^{7}}{42}+\cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the first two terms of this series, we estimate that
\[
\int_{0}^{1 / 2} e^{-t^{2}} d t \approx \frac{1}{2}-\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)=\frac{11}{24}
\]
\item[(d)] \(\left|\int_{0}^{1 / 2} e^{-t^{2}} d t-\frac{11}{24}\right|<\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{5} \cdot \frac{1}{10}=\frac{1}{320}<\frac{1}{200}\), since
\(\int_{0}^{1 / 2} e^{-t^{2}} d t=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2 n+1}}{n!(2 n+1)}\), which is an alternating series with individual terms that decrease in absolute value to 0 .
\end{itemize}
